planting.note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; set out into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after nights stay reliably above 55°F. Kermit thrives in Gulf South heat and humidity, continuing to produce heavily through the hottest part of summer.

directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; harvest young at golf-ball to ping-pong-ball size for the crisp, mild, seed-free texture prized in Thai cooking. Kermit is a small, round Thai eggplant with pale green skin streaked and mottled with cream-white striping, borne in heavy clusters on compact, productive plants that thrive in hot, humid conditions. The firm, dense flesh has very few seeds when harvested young and holds its shape well in curries, stir-fries, and stews — traditional uses in Thai cuisine, where round green eggplants are added whole or halved directly into simmering curry. Its heat tolerance and continuous production over a long summer season make it an excellent, prolific choice for Gulf South vegetable gardens, zone 4–12.

planting.note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; set out into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun once nights stay reliably above 55°F. Harvest fruit when glossy and firm, before the skin dulls and yellows, which signals overripeness and increasing bitterness.

directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; pick fruit young and glossy for the mildest, sweetest flavor and fewest seeds. Casper is a classic heirloom eggplant producing smooth, pure ivory-white, oblong fruit with tender skin that needs no peeling, and notably mild, sweet, non-bitter flesh that browns less than purple varieties once cut — a practical advantage for dishes where appearance matters, like gratins or stuffed preparations. The productive, well-branched plants set fruit reliably over a long summer season and are less prone to the bitterness that can develop in some eggplant varieties under stress. Its striking white color and mild flavor make it a favorite for gardeners wanting a visually distinctive eggplant with excellent kitchen versatility, zone 4–12.

planting.note: Direct sow after all frost danger has passed and soil has warmed to at least 70°F, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; give vines 8–10 feet of room to sprawl.

directions: Sow in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; keep evenly watered through fruit set and ease off as melons near ripeness to concentrate sugars. Stone Mountain is a classic early 20th-century Southern heirloom watermelon, grown for generations across the South for its large, oblong, dark green fruit and exceptionally sweet, deep red, fine-grained flesh with relatively small seed count for an old-time variety. The vigorous vines are productive and well adapted to the long, hot growing season of the Gulf South, and the tough rind travels and stores reasonably well for a heritage variety, a trait that made it a popular market melon in the era before modern shipping cultivars took over. Its rich, old-fashioned flavor and reliable performance in southern heat and humidity have kept it a favorite among heirloom gardeners who want the taste of a bygone-era watermelon, zone 4–11.

planting.note: Start seeds indoors 10–12 weeks before the last frost with bottom heat, since Capsicum chinense germinates slowly; transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after nights stay reliably above 55°F.

directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; the plants are productive and reasonably compact, doing well in raised beds or large containers. Trinidad Seasoning Pepper is a habanero-relative (Capsicum chinense) grown not for heat but for its intense, distinctively fruity, floral habanero-type aroma without the accompanying pungency — a genetic quirk that produces essentially all of the characteristic C. chinense flavor with almost none of the capsaicin heat. It is a foundational ingredient in Trinidadian and broader Caribbean cooking, where it is blended into 'green seasoning' marinades, curries, and sauces to deliver deep habanero-family flavor that can be used generously without overwhelming heat. The wrinkled, lantern-shaped fruits ripen from green through yellow, orange, or red depending on the specific strain. An essential, distinctive pepper for gardeners interested in Caribbean cuisine who want the flavor of a habanero without the fire, zone 8–11.
sources: Trinidad and Tobago Ministry of Agriculture

planting.note: Start seeds indoors 10–12 weeks before the last frost with steady bottom heat near 85°F, since superhot Capsicum chinense types germinate slowly and unevenly; transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after nights stay reliably above 60°F.

directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; handle ripe fruit with gloves and avoid touching eyes or skin, since the extreme capsaicin content can cause burns even from brief contact. 7 Pot Pepper is a legendary superhot pepper from Trinidad, named for the traditional claim that a single pod is potent enough to season seven pots of stew — a nod to its extreme heat, which commonly measures in the range of 800,000 to over 1,000,000 Scoville heat units, placing it among the hottest peppers ever recorded alongside its close relatives Trinidad Scorpion and Trinidad Moruga Scorpion. The gnarled, bumpy, lantern-shaped pods ripen from green to a deep, glossy red and carry a fruity, floral Capsicum chinense aroma beneath the ferocious heat, making it prized by hot sauce makers who want maximum intensity along with genuine habanero-family flavor complexity. A serious specialty pepper for heat enthusiasts only, best grown where its extended season can be accommodated, zone 8–11.
sources: Chile Pepper Institute, New Mexico State University
Trinidad and Tobago Ministry of Agriculture
